questions.title: What standard do appellate courts use when reviewing adequacy of a federal criminal indictment?
questions.question_body: I am reading United States v. Constantinescu where the Fifth Circuit says it reviews sufficiency 'de novo.' I am not clear on what this standard entails. Specifically, does the appellate court treat every allegation in an indictment as true? What elements must be alleged for an offense such as 18 U.S.C. § 1348? How does concern about 'double jeopardy defense' factor into assessing whether an indictment is sufficient? I would appreciate an explanation.

questions.title: How do Ciminelli's 'right-to-control' rejection and Kousisis's 'fraudulent-inducement' approval differ, and why does it matter for securities-fraud charges?
questions.question_body: In Constantinescu the district court dismissed because it thought defendants only deprived followers of valuable economic information—a situation described in Ciminelli's right-to-control theory—and then Fifth Circuit reversed applying Kousisis's fraudulent-inducement theory. I am confused about several points: What is meant by traditional property interest versus right-to-control? Why does fraudulent inducement count as distinct enough after Ciminelli rejected right-to-control claims? And how should prosecutors draft allegations so they fall within one theory rather than another? Understanding this distinction would clarify why this indictment survived dismissal.

questions.title: Does posting false statements about a stock on social media satisfy the 'scheme to defraud' element under 18 U.S.C. § 1348?
questions.question_body: The opinion states that defendants posted false and misleading information so that other investors were induced to purchase securities, thereby satisfying a scheme requirement under 18 U.S.C. § 1348. My questions are: Is merely disseminating misinformation enough to constitute a scheme, or must there be additional conduct such as actual purchase or sale? How have courts addressed social-media communications when defining a scheme in wire or fraud cases? Does the fact that followers voluntarily acted affect whether a scheme exists? I want to understand how courts evaluate 'scheme' in modern online contexts.

questions.title: Is an actual economic loss required for liability under the fraudulent-inducement theory of federal fraud statutes?
questions.question_body: Kousisis held that liability attaches even when plaintiff suffers no net pecuniary loss because defendant sought only money or property. Yet I am still uncertain about two things: Does fraudulent-inducement liability attach if victims receive market-value securities so they suffer no economic loss? How do courts treat situations where parties exchange money or property of equal value? Are there limits on imposing fraud liability when there is no demonstrable loss? Clarification on how loss—or lack thereof—impacts fraudulent-inducement claims would help.

questions.title: What elements must be pled in an indictment charging conspiracy to commit securities fraud under 18 U.S.C. § 1349?
questions.question_body: The case includes charges of conspiracy to commit securities fraud alongside substantive fraud counts, yet defendants argue those counts were insufficiently pled. I need help understanding what factual allegations are required at pleading stage for a § 1349 charge: What must be alleged regarding agreement among conspirators and any overt act? Must each conspirator's individual intent be pleaded separately or can it be inferred from collective conduct? Have recent Supreme Court decisions altered pleading standards for conspiracy in federal fraud cases? Clarifying these points would explain why some courts dismiss conspiracy indictments while others uphold them.

questions.title: Do social-media followers constitute 'persons' with protected property interests under 18 U.S.C. § 1348, and how is their property interest evaluated?
questions.question_body: The Fifth Circuit treats defendants' followers as victims whose money or property was obtained through deceit pursuant to § 1348's reference to 'any person.' I am uncertain about several aspects: Does 'any person' extend to anonymous online followers who might never be individually identified? What constitutes a protected property interest for those followers—does merely holding cash used to buy securities qualify? How have courts handled victim identification in large internet-based pump-and-dump schemes? Understanding victim standing would clarify why this indictment was deemed sufficient.

questions.title: After an appellate reversal on indictment insufficiency, what actions may a district court take on remand without violating double jeopardy?
questions.question_body: The Fifth Circuit reversed the dismissal and remanded for further proceedings based on finding that the indictment sufficiently alleged scheme and intent elements. I wonder what procedural options are available now: Must the district court simply reinstate all counts exactly as originally pleaded, or can it amend the indictment to add more factual detail? Are there limits on amendment if new allegations are introduced after reversal? How does double jeopardy protect defendants from being tried again on essentially the same insufficient charge?
